messages.body_plain:
Dear Professor Terrence,

I hope you are very well.

I have some questions regarding comparison of non-nested models obtained by CFA:

Q1: Is it appropriate to compare (in a descriptive way) fit indexes like CFI, TLI, GFI, AGFI, RMSEA, SRMR?
Q2: Is it appropriate to compare (in a descriptive way) indexes like AIC and BIC?
Q3: What about the Vuong’s test? Do you recommend it?
Q4: Do you recommend any tutorial or papers to read about non-nested models comparison?
Q5: Do you recommend any package in R to make comparison of non-nested models?
Q6: If Vuong's test is appropriate, do you recommend any package in R to perform it?

Thanks in advance.

El mar, 10 nov 2020 a las 14:46, Terrence Jorgensen (<tjorge...@gmail.com>) escribió:

> > I came across this article that was very helpful, especially in explaining how thresholds figure into invariance testing: https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/681607
>
> I would be skeptical of the value of that tutorial.  It propagates the misunderstanding(s) that Wu & Estabrook (2016 <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5458787/>) have tried to clear up.  Namely, as I stated above: without equal thresholds, the latent item responses are not on linked scales, so loadings are not comparable.  The article you link to talks about simultaneously constraining thresholds and loadings (and intercepts, by virtue of not freeing them: another misunderstanding they propagate), which is fine, it just provides a single omnibus test of scalar invariance relative to configural invariance.  In comparison, they free loadings first, then thresholds, which is problematic for the reason in bold above.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

messages.subject: Re: Latent Growth Curve Model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence,

Thank you very much for your answer. It helped a lot.

Is there a way to run a double latent growth model in Lavaan?
I would like to use boredom factor scores instead of manifest boredom means. In my mind it should look like this:

latent_boredom_growth <- '
boredom_0 =~ bos1_0 + bos2_0 + bos3_0 + bos4_0 + bos5_0 + bos6_0; #latent boredom
boredom_1 =~ bos1_1 + bos2_1 + bos3_1 + bos4_1 + bos5_1 + bos6_1;
boredom_2 =~ bos1_2 + bos2_2 + bos3_2 + bos4_2 + bos5_2 + bos6_2;

i =~ 1*boredom_0 + 1*boredom_1 + 1*boredom_2; # intercept
s =~ 0*boredom_0 + 1*boredom_1 + 2*boredom_2; # slope
'
boredom_growth_model = growth(latent_boredom_growth, data=lavan)

But this results in an error:

In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.

Thanks again and kind regards,
Manuel

Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Freitag, 13. November 2020 um 11:59:12 UTC+1:
> > Am I doing this right?
> Looks right.
> > How do I interpret the output?
> https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/growth.html
> Try Googling for more tutorials about growth curves in lavaan, like this one: https://quantdev.ssri.psu.edu/tutorials/growth-modeling-chapter-10-growth-models-nonlinearity-time
>
> > Why are all intercepts 0?
> They aren't.  Only the indicators have intercepts == 0 because their means are reproduces as functions of the growth parameters.  The growth parameter means are merely very close to zero (try adding the argument nd=7 for the summary() to print up to 7 digits of precision).  Slopes nearly zero seems very consistent with the dark blue line in your plot being almost flat.  The plot indicates your (unconditional) average intercept should be somewhere between 2 and 3; however,  you have several predictors of the growth factors.  Thus, the intercepts are the mean level and change when all those predictors == 0.  Does that make sense for your data?
> > What does it mean that intercept, slope, and quadratic slope are not significant?
> It implies those parameters are consistent with a population parameter == 0.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject: Re: Latent Growth Curve Model
messages.body_plain:
Manuel

If you want to do a Growth curve with factors, you first have to establsih longitudinal strong measurement invariance for the Boredom_0, boredom_1, and boredom_2 factors.

Steps:
- Configural model: The factor model with no equality constrint over time. Using fixed variance identification method
- Weak invariance: Equate factor loadings across time, freely estimate the variance at time 2 and 3, keep the variance of time 1 fixed to 1
- Strong invariance: equate item intercepts over time, freely estimate the mean of time 2 and 3, keep the mean at time 1 fixed at 0

Between each step you compare the model to the previous model, to see if the constraints decrease fit substantially

After that you can use the factors from the Strong invariance model for the growth curve

messages.body_plain:
Manuel,

I suspect you're running into issues with the factor intercepts.

I'm not sure whether the growth() function can do this, but the sem()
function could. Then if you specify scalar invariance on the boredom
factors as Mauricio mentioned, then

boredom_0 ~ 0*1
boredom_1 ~ 0*1
boredom_2 ~ 0*1
i ~ 1
s ~ 1

That should get you on the right track.

messages.body_plain:
> lavaan WARNING: trouble constructing W matrix; used generalized inverse for A11 submatrix

> I'm struggling to understand the earlier error for 'trouble constructing W matrix' and haven't been able to find much guidance online - can anyone help with this please?

Looks like the weight matrix used in the default DWLS estimator was not positive definite, so lavaan needed to obtain its generalized (Moore-Penrose) inverse using the ginv() function instead of solve().

If you want to investigate why, you can extract the weight matrix using lavInspect(fit, "WLS.V")

The mean and variance of a latent variable are arbitrary because they
are, definitionally, not measured on any scale. There are some common
options for setting the scaling.

What does your cfa() call look like? If you set std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE in your
function call, then you should expect a mean of about 0 and an SD of
about 1 in the factor scores (where the "true" latent has exactly 0
and 1).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Iraida,

Chi-squared statistic is influenced by sample size. You have more than 1800 cases, the chi-squared test is too sensitive and will basically always be significant, no matter what model you have. In this case, you can just ignore that (but still report them later) and interpret the other fit indices. (CFI, TLI, RMSEA & SRMR).

Cheers,
Hsin-Rui Lin

messages.subject: Re: Testing measurement/structural invariance
messages.body_plain:
> 2. loadings + intercepts (scalar)

> ...

> 8. loadings + intercepts + regressions

As long as you mean indicator intercepts in Step 2 and intercepts of endogenous common factors in Step 8, then that looks fine to me.

Further, if Step 7's H0 is rejected, then you can also separately test lv.variances without constraining lv.covariances.  Possibly homoskedasticity holds but groups have unequal correlations.  Or possibly homoskedasticity holds for some factors but not others, in which case you can test equality of covariances among homoskedastic factors, but would need phantom constructs to test correlations among (homo- and) heteroskedastic factors.

> More to step 8, I noticed that (for the non-reference groups) the unstandardised latent variable intercepts of exogenous variables shown in the summary output are the same as lavInspect (fit.model, "mean.lv <http://mean.lv>"). However, for endogenous latent variables as well as mediating latent variables, the intercepts shown are different between the summary output and "mean.lv <http://mean.lv>". Is it because one is the unadjusted mean ("mean.lv <http://mean.lv>" approach, not controlled for predictors) and the other is the adjusted mean (summary output, controlled for predictors)?

Correct, "mean.lv <http://mean.lv>" returns model-implied latent-variable grand means, not the intercepts (the latter of which are the model parameters).

A variable's intercept is always interpreted as its expected value when its predictor(s) == 0, so an intercept is only an "adjusted mean" (as the term is used in texts about ANCOVA) if the predictors' GRAND means happen to be zero (i.e., in all groups).  Likewise, variable's intercept is its grand mean (in any particular group) only when the variable has no predictor(s) OR its predictors' means all == 0 (in that group).

> For categorical indicators -- objective: compare latent means for one measurement model (one latent factor with both binary and polytomous indicators):

How many categories does the polytomous indicators have?  If only 3, then your sequence below is fine, but your configural model can already constrain thresholds to equality (it is statistically equivalent to equating the intercepts and latent scales, which is the default).

> Using the Wu and Estabrook (2016) approach and measEq.syntax function to generate correct lavaan model syntax (parameterization = "delta" ):
> 1. configural model: (ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu", group.equal="configural")

Don't set group.equal= to anything if you are constraining anything.  "configural" is not a type of parameter.

> 2. metric model:  (ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu", group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings")) -- this model constrains intercept as zero for the reference group and free the other groups.

If your polytomous indicators have > 3 categories, you can separately test equality of thresholds first, then additionally constrain loadings (of items whose thresholds are invariant).  But other than being more informative about the type of DIF, I don't think there is a practical advantage to knowing whether there is DIF in thresholds vs loadings.  But the latter are only comparable when thresholds are equal.

> 3. scalar model: (ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat="Wu", group.equal=c("thresholds","loadings","intercepts")) -- this model essentially constrains intercepts as zero for all groups.
> If the scalar model holds, it is possible to compare latent means across groups.

Yes, although partial scalar invariance is also sufficient.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Error from multi-group analysis
messages.body_plain:
> I have some questions regarding comparison of non-nested models obtained by CFA:

We were discussing measurement-invariance models above, which should be nested (otherwise, something is misspecified).  But perhaps you are not talking about testing invariance.

> Q1: Is it appropriate to compare (in a descriptive way) fit indexes like CFI, TLI, GFI, AGFI, RMSEA, SRMR?

Not the way it is described in 99.9% of the SEM literature.  Most fit indices were not designed for model comparison, and the "change in" a fit index has never stood up to even minor scrutiny.

RMSEA can be calculated using the chi-squared (and df) difference, which was called the root deterioration per restriction (RDR) in the long-long-ago literature.  It was abandoned early on because its sampling distribution tends to be quite erratic, just like RMSEA's for any model with few df or small N.

Incremental fit indices (CFI, TLI) are a notable exception.  If you read the source proposing them (link <https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.88.3.588>), they can be used to compare the fit of any set of nested or nonnested models, on the condition that the null model (baseline.model= argument in the fitIndices() function) used to calculate them is nested within each of the hypothesized models being compared (all of which, by definition, are nested within the same saturated model).

> Q2: Is it appropriate to compare (in a descriptive way) indexes like AIC and BIC?

Information criteria were developed specifically to aid model comparison, but they are only available using a likelihood-based estimator, not least-squares estimators.  So in the latter case, only incremental fit indices might be an option.

> Q3: What about the Vuong’s test? Do you recommend it?

messages.body_plain:
> the chi-squared test is too sensitive and will basically always be significant, no matter what model you have

I object to this mischaracterization.  The chi-squared statistic is exactly as sensitive as it should be to maximize power (i.e., "sensitivity") given the chosen Type I error rate.  And if your model is exactly correct, N has no effect on the rejection rate; it will be nominal, assuming your model's assumptions are met (not just the constraints, but normality, etc.).  This is how a test statistic is supposed to behave.  You use chi-squared to assess statistical significance, not practical significance.

That being said, chi-squared can be statistically significant when there is an egregious misspecification, but also when there are many minor (arguably ignorable) misspecifications that accumulate in the single test statistic.  I agree you probably have a lot of power to detect the set of minor discrepancies you see in the matrix of standardized residuals, and I would conclude that the latter (which are standardized effect sizes, that should always accompany a test of statistical significance) indicate the degree to which the H0 of perfect fit (which you rejected) is false appears to be of little practical importance.

I'm not trying to be overly pedantic, but this is something I have to clarify about chi-squared almost every time I review a paper using SEM.  The limitation of the chi-squared test is not the statistic's behavior, but rather how important it is to the researcher that its H0 be exactly true.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

El vie, 4 dic 2020 a las 8:55, Terrence Jorgensen (<tjorge...@gmail.com>) escribió:

> > I have some questions regarding comparison of non-nested models obtained by CFA:
>
> We were discussing measurement-invariance models above, which should be nested (otherwise, something is misspecified).  But perhaps you are not talking about testing invariance.
>
> > Q1: Is it appropriate to compare (in a descriptive way) fit indexes like CFI, TLI, GFI, AGFI, RMSEA, SRMR?
>
> Not the way it is described in 99.9% of the SEM literature.  Most fit indices were not designed for model comparison, and the "change in" a fit index has never stood up to even minor scrutiny.
>
> RMSEA can be calculated using the chi-squared (and df) difference, which was called the root deterioration per restriction (RDR) in the long-long-ago literature.  It was abandoned early on because its sampling distribution tends to be quite erratic, just like RMSEA's for any model with few df or small N.
>
> Incremental fit indices (CFI, TLI) are a notable exception.  If you read the source proposing them (link <https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.88.3.588>), they can be used to compare the fit of any set of nested or nonnested models, on the condition that the null model (baseline.model= argument in the fitIndices() function) used to calculate them is nested within each of the hypothesized models being compared (all of which, by definition, are nested within the same saturated model).
>
> > Q2: Is it appropriate to compare (in a descriptive way) indexes like AIC and BIC?
>
> Information criteria were developed specifically to aid model comparison, but they are only available using a likelihood-based estimator, not least-squares estimators.  So in the latter case, only incremental fit indices might be an option.
>
> > Q3: What about the Vuong’s test? Do you recommend it?
>

messages.subject: Re: predict factor scores from CFA
messages.body_plain:
The most common other option to set the scaling is a unit (1.00)
loading to one of the indicators. lavaan, like most SEM software,
defaults to the first indicator. So if you look at your unstandardized
results without std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, you will probably see a loading of 1.00 for
b13 on TCN, for b36 for MES, etc.

You haven't changed how you're scaling the mean (default in a
single-group model is factor means constrained to zero), so it's still
zero, but the variance will differ depending on the indicator with the
fixed loading. That's why for many purposes std.lv <http://std.lv>=T is more
convenient for a CFA (it can get a bit messier for SEM).

But factor scores are impure reflections of factors, so even though
the *factor* has M=0 SD=1 (i.e., is standardized), the observed factor
scores will not be exactly M=0 SD=1, though they should be in the
ballpark.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

I am running a second-degree polynomial trajectory model over 50 imputed datasets (N=226) using fun="sem" in runMI() (semTools v.0.5-3). I'm running into an error when I use MLR.

First, when I run the model on a single 50*N dataset with either ML or MLR, everything works as expected, so I don't think the model syntax (pasted at end) is the problem.

With ML:

stai <- runMI(fivepoint, data=distress.mi, fun="sem")

I get 11 warnings from runMI, none of which seems critical.

summary(stai) notes all 50 converged and a couple of Heywood cases, and, after appropriate-seeming model output, two warnings I can't parse. I'm including them here for any diagnostic value:

*******
Convergence information:
The model converged on 50 imputed data sets

Heywood cases detected for data set(s) 18, 30
These are not necessarily a cause for concern, unless a pooled estimate is also a Heywood case.

<model output, no Heywood>

Warning messages:
1: In if (attr(x, "information") == "observed") { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
2: In cbind(c1, c2, deparse.level = 0) :
  number of rows of result is not a multiple of vector length (arg 1)
******

When I change to MLR
stai <- runMI(fivepoint, data=distress.mi, fun="sem", estimator="MLR")

I get the same 11 warnings, but summary(stai) returns an error, one of the same warnings, and no results:

******
The model converged on 50 imputed data sets

Heywood cases detected for data set(s) 18, 30
These are not necessarily a cause for concern, unless a pooled estimate is also a Heywood case.

Rubin's (1987) rules were used to pool point and SE estimates across 50 imputed data sets, and to calculate degrees of freedom for each parameter's t test and CI.

Parameter Estimates:

Error in if (attr(x, "se") == "robust.huber.white" && attr(x, "information.meat") !=  :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
In addition: Warning message:
In if (attr(x, "information") == "observed") { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
*****************

I'd appreciate any help.

Pat

fivepoint <- '
m3 ~ BISQ_sleep_Arrangement_2opt_3m_c + Day_breastfeeding_3m_c
m6 ~ BISQ_sleep_Arrangement_2opt_6m_c + Day_breastfeeding_6m_c

q =~ .6944*m0 + .25*m3 + .0625*m6 + .0625*m12 + .5625*m18

m0 + m3 + m6 + m12 + m18 ~ 0*1
i + s + q ~ 1
i + s + q ~ Infant_gender_c + F_PR_education_c + F_PR_age_c_s + M_PR_education_c + M_PR_age_c_s
i ~~ s + q
s ~~ q
'

> The most common other option to set the scaling is a unit (1.00)

> ballpark.

messages.subject: Re: Scales y*
messages.body_plain:
AFAIK the Scales Y* correspond to the variance of the underlying latent response variable that is assumed to treat ordinal data. I do not find any documentation or reference about how to modify them though, so I also hop on this question. For example, when using the Millsap-Tein (2004) identification, I see that they are still all constrained to 1, whereas the definition (p.485) explicitly says that only one group should have the VarCov* Matrix set to identity.

messages.subject: Re: Factor scores in using lavPredict()
messages.body_plain:
> Could you share the arguments to have the factor scores in the scale of the indicators?

You can't.  Marker-variable and effects-coding methods do not transfer the observed-scale units to the latent variable, unless error variances are zero.  The common factor doesn't have a scale because we haven't directly measured it, and it is only a component of the observed indicators.

https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/1082-989X.7.2.210

> How can I set the factor scale with 'effect coding method of identification'?

See the effect.coding= argument's description in the ?lavOptions help page.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Scales y*
messages.body_plain:
> is there any reference for the "scales y*" section in the output of cfa when using parameterization="theta" and how is it calculated?

Regardless of the parameterization, the scaling factor is the reciprocal of the marginal SD of y*

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf  (see eq. 23)

> For parametrization="delta", I know it is set to 1 by default.

And 1 / 1 == 1, so it is difficult to infer from the output in this convenient case.  But y* scaling factors could be fixed to any other value under the delta parameterization, or freely estimated given sufficient constraints on thresholds.  Delta parameterization just means the scaling factors are parameters, instead of merely implied by other model parameters.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Efficient Scripting: Multiple Constraints in a SEM
messages.subject_clean: Efficient Scripting: Multiple Constraints in a SEM
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone

Does anyone know how to fix the covariances of more than two exogenous variables in a SEM at zero in one line (without the "orthogonal" argument)?

My extensive script with constraints over multiple lines is (simplified):

model <- '
PERT   =~ pdt1 + pdt2 + pdt3                  # PERT is a "pure" enogenous latent variable
UB       =~ ubp1 + ubp2 + ubt1 + ubt2     # UB is endogenous and exogenous

GST    =~ gstp1 + gstp2 + gstp3             # GST, SaC are exogenous latent variables
SaC     =~ sacp1 + sacp2 + sacp3

PERT  ~ UB + GST                                 # PERT is regressed on UB, GST
UB       ~ SaC                                          # UB is regressed on SaC

GST  ~~ 0*UB                                       # GST and UB are uncorrelated
GST  ~~ 0*SaC                                     # GST and SaC are uncorrelated
 '
After having tried out, I guess the two blue lines can be integrated in one line:

      GST ~~ 0*UB + 0*SaC

Even though this seems to work fine (same results as the extensive script), the plus sign "+" irritates me because covariances are not "added up". Therefore I would like to check if anyone can verify my guess.

Any feedback is much appreciated!

Best whishes
Boris

PS: I cannot use the "orthogonal" argument, because in other, more comprehensive models some of the exogenous variables need to correlate.

Hi Pat,

I have seen this problem a couple times before (defaulting back to the lavaanList method, from which lavaan.mi inherits), and have not yet been able to reproduce it or discover a reason for it.  Try re-installing semTools in a fresh R session, then restarting R before running your model again.  Try only loading semTools and running that part, so no other packages are loaded (other than the base, as well as lavaan automatically and all its dependencies).  Also, see if this happens to you even with the help-page examples (again, start in a fresh R session), which might help narrow down what else in the environment is interfering with R finding the semTools path to lavaan.mi methods.

If it still occurs, please post your sessionInfo() output.  I might need output to see if I can reproduce it on my machine, so if you can find a brief enough example that generates your error using data you can share, that could help me track down the problem.

As far as obtaining your output in any case:  Even for the person for whom nothing solved the problem, she was able to access the lavaan.mi methods by explicitly calling them via getMethod().

getMethod(summary, "lavaan.mi")(anx_bisqdur_lag)

Another option is to access the hidden functions behind those methods.  I've used the S3 method naming convention, so:

semTools:::summary.lavaan.mi(anx_bisqdur_lag)

Best,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
>  #If I were to estimate ChiSq using the model and observed cov matrices

> S <- cov(d); S

Note that in accordance with asymptotic theory, lavaan rescales this sample covariance to divide the sum of squares and cross-products by N rather than N - 1, unless you override the default by setting sample.cov.rescale=FALSE (see ?lavOptions).

Random tip:  you can print when assigning by doing so within parentheses:

(S <- cov(d))

> #Without scaling of number of observation, Fit function
> fitf <- log(det(C)) - log(det(S)) + sum(diag(S %*% solve(C))) - n

Yes, although you are missing a term for the mean structure (if your model has a non-saturated mean structure)

Note that this is the average -2*log(likelihood-ratio)s comparing your fitted model to a saturated model.  Multiplying a mean by N gives the sum of casewise -2*log(likelihood-ratio)s, which is distributed as a chi-squared random variable.

> likl = log(det(C)) + sum(diag(S%*%solve(C))) - log(det(S)) - n

No, the fit function does not return the log(likelihood) of the fitted model.  That can be found with logLik(fit)

> bic = -2*log(likl) + log(N)*((count_free_parameters(fit1) - (nfac == 0, 1,0))
> Error: unexpected ',' in "bic = -2*log(likl) + log(N)*((count_free_parameters(fit1) - (nfac == 0,"

As the error message indicates, there is a problematic comma. What do you mean to do with this bit of syntax?

- (nfac == 0, 1,0)

Did you mean to use the ifelse() function with that test of nfac==0, returning a dummy code?

>  chisq = likl*(N-1)

Note also that lavaan multiplies the fit function by N, in accordance with asymptotic normal theory, unless you override the default by setting likelihood="wishart"

I suspect if you multiply your S by (N-1)/N, and multiply your fit function by N, then your results should match lavaan's chi-squared.  If you have a follow-up, please use/adapt a help-page example so we can also run your syntax.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Moderation in Actor-Partner Interdependence Model
messages.body_plain:
> individuals nested in couples

But the APIM in SEM puts dyads in wide format, so there is no nesting of rows within dyads (members of dyads instead have data stored in different columns, as your variables indicate).

> I would now like to add a categorical level-2 moderator, but I am unsure how to go about.

You can either include its dummy code(s) as exogenous predictor(s), which is the familiar approach from regression models:  https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

Or you can use it to run a multigroup model:  https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html
In the latter, moderation is implicit when a parameter (e.g., regression slope) is allowed to vary across groups.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: Efficient Scripting: Multiple Constraints in a SEM
messages.body_plain:
> Does anyone know how to fix the covariances of more than two exogenous variables in a SEM at zero in one line (without the "orthogonal" argument)?

It doesn't need to be on one line, if that's easier.  Syntax can be a character vector of length > 1, so you can use paste() to assemble different script components pretty automatically with variable names.  An adaptation from the ?cfa help page:

HS.model <- c(paste0("visual =~ x", 1:3), paste0("textual =~ x", 4:6), paste0("speed =~ x", 7:9))
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit)

The same principle works for specifying a set of orthogonalities.  You could even do so for an entire (sub)matrix using outer() with paste():

varnames <- paste0("x", 1:6)
covstruc <- outer(varnames, varnames, function(x, y) paste(x, "~~", y))
satMod <- c(paste(varnames, "~ 1"), # mean structure
            covstruc[lower.tri(covstruc, diag = TRUE)]) # cov structure
cat(satMod, sep = "\n")

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: How does sem() calculate the variances of categorical endogenous variables which depends on a mediator?
messages.subject_clean: How does sem() calculate the variances of categorical endogenous variables which depends on a mediator?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to understand how lavaan calculates variances of a categorical endogenous variable, when the categorical output depends on a mediator variable.

I have this simple model for illustration:
dat <- data.frame(a=rnorm(1000000))
dat$b <- dat$a*0.80+rnorm(1000000,0,0.1)
dat$c <- factor(ifelse(+5-2*dat$b+rnorm(1000000,0,1)>0,1,0),ordered = TRUE)
sem('b~a
            c~b', data=dat, meanstructure=TRUE)

which gives the following output:Regressions:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
  b ~
    a                 0.800    0.000 8027.399    0.000
  c ~
    b                -1.970    0.019 -105.891    0.000

Intercepts:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
   .b                -0.000    0.000   -0.538    0.590
   .c                 0.000

Thresholds:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    c|t1             -4.936    0.034 -146.734    0.000

Variances:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
   .b                 0.010    0.000  707.188    0.000
   .c                 0.961

Scales y*:
                   Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
    c                 1.000

I am wondering how the estimate for the variance of the categorical variable is calculated (marked in yellow). If b was an exogenous variable, the variance of c would be 1. But here, b is endogenous (and a mediator) and the variance is 0.961. I understand that the threshold estimates for c are obtained from the intercept of a ordered probit-regression model. But, how is the variance here calculated?

Could someone help me here please?
(I think a similar question remained unsanswered in this post <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/MJ2QYGxyaZE/m/PYuW251wCAAJ>)

Thank you very much!

messages.subject_clean: How are CFI and TLI nd RMSEA and SRMR calculated in lavaan?
messages.body_plain:
The cool thing about open source code (like lavaan) is that if you want to know how something is done, you don't need to take anyone's word for it, you can go and look.

The file to look at is:
https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/blob/d7a6ea7ed5c1b21e3e5f7a909d78788579f300f7/R/lav_fit_measures.R

And the gist of the code for the lower CI of RMSEA is (pulling out all of the error checking and stuff):
lower.lambda <- function(lambda) {
  pchisq(X2, df=df, ncp=lambda) - 0.95
 }
lambda.l <- try(uniroot(f=lower.lambda, lower=0, upper=X2)$root, silent=TRUE)
GG <- 0
["rmsea.ci.lower"] <- ( lambda.l/((N-GG)*df) ) * sqrt(G)

(Where G is the number of groups, usually 1).

And here's CFI:

t1 <- max( c(X2 - df, 0) )
                t2 <- max( c(X2 - df, X2.null - df.null, 0) )
                if(isTRUE(all.equal(t1,0)) &&
                   isTRUE(all.equal(t2,0))) {
                    indices["cfi"] <- 1
                } else {
                    indices["cfi"] <- 1 - t1/t2
                }

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure what you're trying to do.

If you want the measures, you can  use the fitMeasures() function to extract them from the fitted model.

 fit <- sem(model, data=PoliticalDemocracy)
fitMeasures(fit)

If you want to calculate them by hand, what information do you want to calculate them from?

If you have X2 = fitted model chi-square, X2.null is null model chi square, df is fitted df, and df.null is null df, then:

t1 <- max( c(X2 - df, 0) )
t2 <- max( c(X2 - df, X2.null - df.null, 0) )

cfi  <- 1 - t1/t2

But you get all those statistics you want using the fitMeasures function, and you can also use that to get CFI.

If you copy and paste my email, which includes explanations, it won't run. :)

If you want to calculate them 'by hand' you're probably better of with a book or article that gives the formulas, your favorite internet search engine can probably help you out. E.g. I typed <rmsea lower confidence interval equation> into my favorite search engine, and found this article: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10062422 (by, amongst others, the author of Lavaan) which contains the formulas.

Hope that helps,

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Latent Growth Curve Model
messages.body_plain:
Manuel

It is not recommended for you to add the factor scores as measured variables, and then run the growth model with them. This goes back into the porblem of factor score indeteminancy and other issues of factor score variability and method.

The recommend steps would be t estimate the growth curve on top of the longitudinal scalar invariance model. This would required you to add 2 pieces to the measurement inavriance model
- The intercept and slope factors define by the first order factors, as you have it
- fix the first order factors means to 0. This way the mean change over time would be only define by the growth curve

Hope this helps

X2 <- fitMeasures(fit)[["chisq"]]

df <- fitMeasures(fit)[["df"]]
df.null <- fitMeasures(fit)[["baseline.df"]]

cfi  <- 1 - t1/t2

X2 <- fitMeasures(fit)[["cfi"]]

But the APIM in SEM puts dyads in wide format, so there is no nesting of rows within dyads (members of dyads instead have data stored in   different columns, as your variables indicate).

messages.subject: Re: Latent Growth Curve Model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Mauricio,

I see. Then I misunderstood you saying I should "use the factors from the Strong invariance model for the growth curve". It also felt unusual.

This is my model for longitudinal scalar invariance and I added the growth curve at the end:

strong_boredom_growth <- '
 # measurement model
 boredom_0 =~ NA*bos1_0 + lambda1*bos1_0 + lambda2*bos2_0 + lambda3*bos3_0 + lambda4*bos4_0 + lambda5*bos5_0+ lambda6*bos6_0
 boredom_1 =~ NA*bos1_1 + lambda1*bos1_1 + lambda2*bos2_1 + lambda3*bos3_1 + lambda4*bos4_1 + lambda5*bos5_1+ lambda6*bos6_1
 boredom_2 =~ NA*bos1_2 + lambda1*bos1_2 + lambda2*bos2_2 + lambda3*bos3_2 + lambda4*bos4_2 + lambda5*bos5_2+ lambda6*bos6_2

 # intercepts
 bos1_0 ~ i1*1
 bos2_0 ~ i2*1
 bos3_0 ~ i3*1
 bos4_0 ~ i4*1
 bos5_0 ~ i5*1
 bos6_0 ~ i6*1
 bos1_1 ~ i1*1
 bos2_1 ~ i2*1
 bos3_1 ~ i3*1
 bos4_1 ~ i4*1
 bos5_1 ~ i5*1
 bos6_1 ~ i6*1
 bos1_2 ~ i1*1
 bos2_2 ~ i2*1
 bos3_2 ~ i3*1
 bos4_2 ~ i4*1
 bos5_2 ~ i5*1
 bos6_2 ~ i6*1

 # unique variances and covariances
 bos1_0 ~~ bos1_0
 bos2_0 ~~ bos2_0
 bos3_0 ~~ bos3_0
 bos4_0 ~~ bos4_0
 bos5_0 ~~ bos5_0
 bos6_0 ~~ bos6_0
 bos1_1 ~~ bos1_1
 bos2_1 ~~ bos2_1
 bos3_1 ~~ bos3_1
 bos4_1 ~~ bos4_1
 bos5_1 ~~ bos5_1
 bos6_1 ~~ bos6_1
 bos1_2 ~~ bos1_2
 bos2_2 ~~ bos2_2
 bos3_2 ~~ bos3_2
 bos4_2 ~~ bos4_2
 bos5_2 ~~ bos5_2
 bos6_2 ~~ bos6_2
 bos1_0 ~~ bos1_1 + bos1_2
 bos2_0 ~~ bos2_1 + bos2_2
 bos3_0 ~~ bos3_1 + bos3_2
 bos4_0 ~~ bos4_1 + bos4_2
 bos5_0 ~~ bos5_1 + bos5_2
 bos6_0 ~~ bos6_1 + bos6_2

 # latent variables means
 boredom_0 ~ 0*1
 boredom_1 ~ 1
 boredom_2 ~ 1

 # latent variables variances and covariances
 boredom_0 ~~ 1*boredom_0
 boredom_1 ~~ boredom_1
 boredom_2 ~~ boredom_2
 boredom_0 ~~ boredom_1
 boredom_0 ~~ boredom_2
 boredom_1 ~~ boredom_2

 # adding the growth model

 i =~ 1*boredom_0 + 1*boredom_1 + 1*boredom_2 # intercept
 s =~ 0*boredom_0 + 1*boredom_1 + 2*boredom_2 # slope
'

# model estimation
boredom_growth_model = growth(strong_boredom_growth, data=df1)

summary(boredom_growth_model)

Unfortunately, this again results in an error:

1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= 1.853961e-18) is close to zero. This may be a symptom that the
    model is not identified.
2: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative

I looked at the summary anyways and attached it as pdf, if this is of any help.

Kind regards,
Manuel

> Manuel

> It is not recommended for you to add the factor scores as measured variables, and then run the growth model with them. This goes back into the porblem of factor score indeteminancy and other issues of factor score variability and method.
>
> The recommend steps would be t estimate the growth curve on top of the longitudinal scalar invariance model. This would required you to add 2 pieces to the measurement inavriance model
> - The intercept and slope factors define by the first order factors, as you have it
> - fix the first order factors means to 0. This way the mean change over time would be only define by the growth curve
>

Terrence Jorgensen schrieb am Mittwoch, 9. Dezember 2020 um 17:08:11 UTC+1:
> > Does anyone know how to fix the covariances of more than two exogenous variables in a SEM at zero in one line (without the "orthogonal" argument)?
>
> It doesn't need to be on one line, if that's easier.  Syntax can be a character vector of length > 1, so you can use paste() to assemble different script components pretty automatically with variable names.  An adaptation from the ?cfa help page:
>
> HS.model <- c(paste0("visual =~ x", 1:3), paste0("textual =~ x", 4:6), paste0("speed =~ x", 7:9))
> fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
> summary(fit)
>
> The same principle works for specifying a set of orthogonalities.  You could even do so for an entire (sub)matrix using outer() with paste():
>
> varnames <- paste0("x", 1:6)
> covstruc <- outer(varnames, varnames, function(x, y) paste(x, "~~", y))
> satMod <- c(paste(varnames, "~ 1"), # mean structure
>             covstruc[lower.tri(covstruc, diag = TRUE)]) # cov structure
> cat(satMod, sep = "\n")
>
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject: nested model
messages.body_plain:
I have three potential moderators (E, S, I), and I want to examine E is a significant moderator above and beyond the influence of these other moderators.

So my advisor told me that I need to use nested models for my research question.  This is what I came up.

1st model : baseline model

2nd model : baseline model +  E

3rd model : baseline model +  E + S

4th model : baseline model + E + S +I

I am just confused about my codes though…

1st model (=baseline) should be:  Y= A +E + S + I + gender + generation

 (Note: A= predictor,  gender, generation = covariates)

2nd model: Y= A +E + A*E +S + I + gender + generation (here I added first interaction term= A*E)

3rd model:  Y= A +E + A*E +S + A*S + I + A*I + gender + generation (added 2nd interaction term= A*S)

4th  model: Y= A +E + A*E +S + A*S + I + A* I + gender + generation ( added 3rd interaction term= A*I)

1. Are these looking correct ? I am not sure what the baseline model should look like….

2. I know I need to us ANOVA to compare model fits, but is there any way that I can get RMSEA, CFI other model fits ?

Any feedback would be greatly appreciated.

# corrected chi-square differences test
CorrDiff <- function(fit.baseline, fit.restricted) # basline = model with less degrees of freedom
{
  Corrc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[6]] # corrected chi-square value
  MLc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[3]] # uncorrected chi-square value
  dfBase <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[4]] # degrees of freedom

  Corrc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[6]]
  MLc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[3]]
  dfRest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[4]]

  c0 <- MLc2Rest / Corrc2Rest
  c1 <- MLc2Base / Corrc2Base
  cd <- (dfRest*c0-dfBase*c1)/(dfRest-dfBase)
  CorrDiff <- (MLc2Rest-MLc2Base)/cd # corrected difference test statistic T_d^*
  dfDiff <- dfRest - dfBase
  pDiff <- 1-pchisq(CorrDiff, dfDiff)
  result <- list(Corr.chisq.difference = CorrDiff,

  return(result)

messages.body_plain:
I haven't been following this thread closely, but what's the benefit of the first right-hand-side term in

boredom_0 =~ NA*bos1_0 + lambda1*bos1_0 +

(and similar for _1 and _2). I can't figure out what it would do, versus

boredom_0 =~ lambda1*bos1_0 +

Also, I'd recommend using the sem() wrapper instead of the growth() wrapper, since growth() is based on, as far as I know, growth of observed variables, not latents. You specify so much else in your model, I think sem() would work fine and be less likely to run into unintended defaults. Though you may need to add:

i ~ 1
s ~ 1

Pat

> # 3. Model Comparison ----------------------------------------------------

> # * 3.1 Steinmetz, 2014 ---------------------------------------------------
>
> # corrected chi-square differences test
> CorrDiff <- function(fit.baseline, fit.restricted) # basline = model with less degrees of freedom
> {
>   Corrc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[6]] # corrected chi-square value
>   MLc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[3]] # uncorrected chi-square value
>   dfBase <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[4]] # degrees of freedom
>
>   Corrc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[6]]
>   MLc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[3]]
>   dfRest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[4]]
>
>   c0 <- MLc2Rest / Corrc2Rest
>   c1 <- MLc2Base / Corrc2Base
>   cd <- (dfRest*c0-dfBase*c1)/(dfRest-dfBase)
>   CorrDiff <- (MLc2Rest-MLc2Base)/cd # corrected difference test statistic T_d^*
>   dfDiff <- dfRest - dfBase
>   pDiff <- 1-pchisq(CorrDiff, dfDiff)

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am currently conducting a mediation SEM using lavaan in R.
However, I’m conducting an integrative data analysis across multiple samples,
and I am wanting to control for the main and interaction effects of sample
(dummy coded variables). I’m running into trouble with creating interaction
terms – it’s fine when creating an interaction term with my dummy coded sample
indicator and another indicator variable in my model, but I can’t seem to
create an interaction term with my dummy coded sample indicator and latent
variables in my model.

I have tried to simply create the term in my model as with
my indicator interaction terms (e.g., DC:Latent Variable) which doesn’t work,
and I’ve tried to create this term outside my model by defining the interaction
(e.g., DCLVX := DC*Latent Variable) and I get the following error:

Error in lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster =
cluster,  :

  lavaan ERROR: missing observed variables in
dataset: EC1_SUP

I have had a browse of the other forum questions, and came
across two solutions, that I’m not sure really get at what I am wanting:

1)      I
know there is the multigroup model approach, but the point of my analyses is to
run a meta-analytic model rather than run the model for individual samples
within my dataset.

2)      I
also read about the indProd function, but from my understanding this would
create interaction terms between my dummy code variable(s) and ALL indicators
of my latent variable(s)? I want to avoid this if possible because I have 20
indicators for my 5 latent variables, and 2 dummy coded variables, which would
give me 100 interaction terms… I don’t think my model can handle all these over
and above the rest of my model parameters. Is there a way to create an
interaction term with the latent variable itself rather than the indicators?

Kind Regards,

Yuthika Girme

Yuthika,

Using the multiple-group approach, you can constrain or release structural paths between groups. Fully constraining them to equality is the no-interaction model. Releasing a given path across groups lets you test sample as a moderator of that path.

Hope that helps,
Pat

messages.subject: Re: How does sem() calculate the variances of categorical endogenous variables which depends on a mediator?
messages.subject_clean: How does sem() calculate the variances of categorical endogenous variables which depends on a mediator?
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, December 9, 2020 at 12:08:25 PM UTC-5 jana...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hello,
>
> I am trying to understand how lavaan calculates variances of a categorical endogenous variable, when the categorical output depends on a mediator variable.
>
> I have this simple model for illustration:
> dat <- data.frame(a=rnorm(1000000))
> dat$b <- dat$a*0.80+rnorm(1000000,0,0.1)
> dat$c <- factor(ifelse(+5-2*dat$b+rnorm(1000000,0,1)>0,1,0),ordered = TRUE)
> sem('b~a
>             c~b', data=dat, meanstructure=TRUE)
>
> which gives the following output:Regressions:
>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
>   b ~
>     a                 0.800    0.000 8027.399    0.000
>   c ~
>     b                -1.970    0.019 -105.891    0.000
>
> Intercepts:
>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
>    .b                -0.000    0.000   -0.538    0.590
>    .c                 0.000
>
> Thresholds:
>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
>     c|t1             -4.936    0.034 -146.734    0.000
>
> Variances:
>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
>    .b                 0.010    0.000  707.188    0.000
>    .c                 0.961
>
> Scales y*:
>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
>     c                 1.000
>
> I am wondering how the estimate for the variance of the categorical variable is calculated (marked in yellow). If b was an exogenous variable, the variance of c would be 1.

The total variance of c is 1 (see its scaling factor; this is the default: parameterization = "delta").  The residual variance of c is thus 1 minus its R-squared (variance explained by its only predictor: b).  Because b is endogenous, its total variance is not a model parameter, so the R-squared is a sum of 2 components:
the squared direct effect of b times b's residual variance
the squared indirect effect of a (via b) times a's variance
Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Hi Terrence

Many thanks for your reply. The documentation link helped me to check the DWLS estimator for my survey data.

Regarding the "right" estimator for 7-point likert scale data: The problem is that several fit indices do not indicate good model fit (cfi, tli, rmsea, srmr) with my data in my bachelor thesis if I use MLR or MLM. So I started researching if other estimators would
make sense too for my model (and get me a better model fit).

I have read your referenced journal articles as well, thank you for providing them.

"When Can Categorical Variables Be Treated as Continuous? A Comparison of Robust Continuous and Categorical SEM Estimation Methods Under Suboptimal Conditions"
recommend cat-LS for data sets containing variables with fewer than 5 categories and ML when there are 5 or more categories, sample size is small, and category thresholds are approximately symmetric.
With 6 –7 categories, results were similar across methods for many conditions; in these cases, either method is acceptable.
"Confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data: Comparing robust maximum likelihood and diagonally weighted least squares"
each estimator has its advantages and disadvantages
study provides conclusive evidence that WLSMV performs uniformly better than MLR in factor loading estimates across all experimental conditions
My conculsion: Based on your sources,  I could also use DWLS for my 7-point liker scale (sample size: 230 participants) to get a better model fit instead of ML. Is that correct?

messages.body_plain:
> My conculsion: Based on your sources,  I could also use DWLS for my 7-point liker scale (sample size: 230 participants) to get a better model fit instead of ML. Is that correct?

No, you do not choose an estimator based on its resulting fit indices.  ML and DWLS don't even use the same criteria (covariance matrix and mean vector vs. polychoric correlation matrix and thresholds), so the fit is not comparable across estimators.

N=230 is far too small for even a small model for DWLS to provide stable results, especially with so many categories.  If your model is large, 230 might still be small for ML, but it shouldn't be as bad as DWLS.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Manova in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I would love to get some help.

I have two independent variables  - x, z. And two dependent variables - y1, Y2. Everything tests on the same people, that is, each subject has scored in all four vars.  My questions:

1. Is it correct to do the analysis like this:
Model <- '
Y1 ~ X + Z
Y2 ~ X + Z '
does Lavaan alone understand that it is repeated measures?

2. Is it possible to say that it is actually MANOVA in SEM? Is there a difference between the two methodological ways of analysis? should I have to use the MANOVA package instead of sem?

3. The situation gets complicated, and I have this analysis for 2 different groups. That means, I have a variable G that has 2 values, and I want the same analysis of no.1 for the two groups but with a statistical comparison between them. How can I do that?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Manova in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
'
1 & 2. Yes, that's a manova.

It takes into account the correlation in the residual variances of Y1 and Y2, and you can do univariate or multivariate tests (I find the SEM framework much more straightforward to understand than manova).

3.  I think that you're talking about a multiple group analysis? I'm not sure. Why not to

Y1 ~ X + Z + G
Y2 ~ X + Z  + G

What do you want to compare?

> > # 3. Model Comparison ----------------------------------------------------
> >
> > # * 3.1 Steinmetz, 2014 ---------------------------------------------------
> >
> > # corrected chi-square differences test
> > CorrDiff <- function(fit.baseline, fit.restricted) # basline = model with less degrees of freedom
> > {
> >   Corrc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[6]] # corrected chi-square value
> >   MLc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[3]] # uncorrected chi-square value
> >   dfBase <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[4]] # degrees of freedom
> >
> >   Corrc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[6]]
> >   MLc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[3]]
> >   dfRest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[4]]
> >
> >   c0 <- MLc2Rest / Corrc2Rest
> >   c1 <- MLc2Base / Corrc2Base
> >   cd <- (dfRest*c0-dfBase*c1)/(dfRest-dfBase)
> >   CorrDiff <- (MLc2Rest-MLc2Base)/cd # corrected difference test statistic T_d^*
> >   dfDiff <- dfRest - dfBase
> >   pDiff <- 1-pchisq(CorrDiff, dfDiff)
> >   result <- list(Corr.chisq.difference = CorrDiff,
> >                  df.difference=dfDiff, p.value=pDiff)
> >   return(result)
> > }
> >
> > # model comparison
> > CorrDiff(fit_configural_boredom, fit_weak_boredom)
> > CorrDiff(fit_weak_boredom, fit_strong_boredom)
> > CorrDiff(fit_strong_boredom, fit_strict_boredom)

> Can I use Lavaan to run this model

Yes

> are there any problems which I don't see right now?

Don't set estimator = "WLS".  lavaan will automatically set it to DWLS (a specific WLS procedure for categorical data) when you declare any endogenous variables as ordered.

Not sure results would be comparable to SPSS PROCESS unless you fit the same models.  For example, lavaan fits a (cumulative) probit regression model to (ordered or binary) outcomes, so you would need to use the same in SPSS for results to be comparable.

messages.subject: Re: Moderation in Actor-Partner Interdependence Model
messages.body_plain:
> Am I correct that moderation does indeed occur

No one can know, but using alpha = .05, you can reject the H0 that the entire set of group-differences is zero.

> but that there is no difference between the regression coefficients in the two groups (values highlighted in yellow)?

The differences are nonzero, but the degree to which they differ from the H0 of no moderation is consistent with what you can expect from sampling error alone when H0 is true.  You are estimating several parameters for such small sample sizes, so you can't expect a lot of power to detect effects that aren't veeery large.

> how would I be able to compute fit indices for each group?

Does it make sense to?  If there are NO equality constraints across groups, then the results would be equivalent if you fit the model separately to each group.  If there are equality constraints across groups, then the chi-squared statistic cannot be partitioned into this or that group's misspecification, so you can't have group-specific indices based on chi-squared.  You can get group-specific standardized/correlation residuals, as well as their average (SRMR / CRMR) from lavResiduals()

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> > > # 3. Model Comparison ----------------------------------------------------
> > >
> > > # * 3.1 Steinmetz, 2014 ---------------------------------------------------
> > >
> > > # corrected chi-square differences test
> > > CorrDiff <- function(fit.baseline, fit.restricted) # basline = model with less degrees of freedom
> > > {
> > >   Corrc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[6]] # corrected chi-square value
> > >   MLc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[3]] # uncorrected chi-square value
> > >   dfBase <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[4]] # degrees of freedom
> > >
> > >   Corrc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[6]]
> > >   MLc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[3]]
> > >   dfRest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[4]]
> > >
> > >   c0 <- MLc2Rest / Corrc2Rest
> > >   c1 <- MLc2Base / Corrc2Base
> > >   cd <- (dfRest*c0-dfBase*c1)/(dfRest-dfBase)
> > >   CorrDiff <- (MLc2Rest-MLc2Base)/cd # corrected difference test statistic T_d^*
> > >   dfDiff <- dfRest - dfBase
> > >   pDiff <- 1-pchisq(CorrDiff, dfDiff)
> > >   result <- list(Corr.chisq.difference = CorrDiff,
> > >                  df.difference=dfDiff, p.value=pDiff)
> > >   return(result)
> > > }
> > >
> > > # model comparison
> > > CorrDiff(fit_configural_boredom, fit_weak_boredom)
> > > CorrDiff(fit_weak_boredom, fit_strong_boredom)

messages.subject: Re: Manova in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
I think the only real difference is that lavaan defaults to a maximum likelihood estimator and MANOVA usually to a least squares estimator. If assumptions are met, these should give essentially the same results. You could explore this by trying different estimators in lavaan and comparing to a MANOVA program's output.

messages.subject: Re: Report results from latent Moderation (probe with wald test)
messages.subject_clean: Report results from latent Moderation (probe with wald test)
messages.body_plain:
> I was wondering whether I only report the significant result of the SEM (beta, p-value) or also the results of the Wald-test (probe2WayMC).

Not sure what your field is, but APA style recommends reporting the parameter along with a measure of uncertainty (SE or CI), its NHST statistic with p value, and a standardized measure of effect size (e.g., the standardized slope in the std.all column).

> And if I report both, could anybody recommend an approach to test the slopes of the interaction with the wald test unarbitrarily? with a latent variable, it's tricky to justify the concrete values I use to probe the interaction, I recon?

It is up to you to decide what values of the moderator are not arbitrary.  The default is the M +/- SD because that is a common convention and captures a good representation of the distribution of the moderator if it is normally distributed.

FYI, don't trust your results yet.  There is a bug in the probe2Way*() functions that causes the estimates and/or SEs to be switched between focal predictor and moderator, depending on the order of variable names specified.  I won't be able to fix the bug until after my teaching wraps up for the semester.  Once I do, I will push a new semTools to CRAN, so you will know the bug is fixed when you can update the package to 0.5-4.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Hi Pat,

Yea, so the fully constrained model was not as good as the default multigroup model that didn't have any constraints, but it wasn't terrible. Keep in mind, I'm trying to conduct a meta-analysis across datasets and so I'm not interested in group differences, but simply want to ensure I'm controlling for dataset source.

Multigroup Analysis without any constraints: CFI = .931, RMSEA = .058
Multigroup Analysis with all constraints: CFI = .876, RMSEA = .071

My syntax for the multigroup analysis with constraints looks like this (below) and it's the bit in bold that appears at the end of my output rather than individually for each group like the rest of the SEM output.

model2 <- '
  #measurement model
  WB =~ lifesat1+lifesat2+lifesat3+lifesat4+lifesat5
  SUP =~ supav1+supav2+supav3+supav4+supav5+supav6+supav7+supav8
  AH =~ AH1+AH2+AH3
  PH =~ PH1+PH2+PH3
  AF =~ AF1+AF2+AF3
  PF =~ PF1+PF2+PF3

  #regressions
  WB ~ c*REL.STATUS + b1*SUP + b2*AH + b3*PH + b4*AF + b5*PF + gender + age_c
  SUP ~ a1*REL.STATUS + gender + age_c
  AH ~ a2*REL.STATUS + gender + age_c
  PH ~ a3*REL.STATUS + gender + age_c
  AF ~ a4*REL.STATUS + gender + age_c
  PF ~ a5*REL.STATUS + gender + age_c
  #stigma to support regressions
  SUP ~ d2*AH + d3*PH + d4*AF + d5*PF
  #residual covariances
  AH ~~ PH + AF + PF
  PH ~~ AF + PF
  AF ~~ PF

  #define direct and indirect pathways
  indirect_sup := a1*b1
  indirect_ah  := a2*b2
  indirect_ph  := a3*b3
  indirect_af  := a4*b4
  indirect_pf := a5*b5
  indirect_ah_sup := a2*d2*b1
  indirect_ph_sup := a3*d3*b1
  indirect_af_sup := a4*d4*b1
  indirect_pf_sup := a5*d5*b1
  direct := c
  total := c + (a1*b1) + (a2*b2) + (a3*b3) + (a4*b4) + (a5*b5) + (a2*d2*b1) + (a3*d3*b1)+ (a4*d4*b1)+ (a5*d5*b1)'

fit1<-sem(model2,data=IDASem, group = "Dataset", group.equal = c("intercepts", "loadings", "means", "residuals", "lv.variances", "lv.covariances", "residual.covariances", "regressions"))

messages.body_plain:
Yuthika,

The multiple-group model, whether constrained or unconstrained, is probably the best way to "control" for dataset source.

If the constrained model does not fit, it indicates heterogeneity by dataset source, which is important to note in a meta-analysis.

However, allowing heterogeneity in the means and intercepts of a path analysis still controls for dataset source, in the sense of applying it as a covariate. If a model with means and intercepts freed fits well, you can still interpret the constrained path coefficients (and therefore the indirect effects) as being homogenous across studies. So I suggest checking that next.

The reason you're only getting one set of indirect effects is that the label constraints are applied across groups. So for indirect_sup, a1 is the a path for all groups because of the way you constrained it in the ~ regression part of the formula--with only one label--and similar for b1. You'd have to have different labels for the paths in different groups to get varying indirect effects, and manage the constraints to equality separately.

Hope that helps,
Pat

messages.subject: Re: standard errors for correlation matrix
messages.body_plain:
I don't think so, but unsolicited advice: Draw conclusions from SEs and p-values of unstandardized coefficients--in this case, covariances, not correlations. SEs on correlations aren't useful anyway, since the correlation coefficient has an asymmetric sampling distribution (a Q distribution, I think? but definitely skewed). The sampling distribution of the covariance isn't normal, either, but isn't usually going to be as bad since it doesn't have a ceiling, but there are still better ways to test it than z-tests.

Pat

messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of Latent Response Fitted Means in an Ordinal CFA
messages.body_plain:
When we fit a CFA model in a measurement model with ordinal indicators, I get that we are trying to reconstruct the observed polychoric (in the case of polytomous variables) correlation matrix. In a model using the delta parametrization constraints, the fitted.values() command returns our model-implied matrix, the means (of the assumed latent normal variables) and the thresholds.

My question is, how can these fitted latent means be interpreted? How can we evaluate the fit of these means, is there a transformation that would make it comparable to the original ordinal scale (assuming that means of Likert items are interpretable)? Is the interpretation dependent on the level of constraints, in the context of a measurement invariance test?

Thank you in advance

messages.subject: Re: Manova in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
In MANOVA, you would do this with an interacting factor. In lavaan, you can either do that (have a product term fo G*X and G*Z, and arguably X*Z and G*X*Z just in case) or have a multiple-group model where you have finer control over what parameters are fixed or freed between groups.

Pat

> I keep getting a scalar 1st order model that fits better than the scalar 2nd order model. Why?

Because you are adding constraints on more parameters.  Comparing any higher-number model to any lower-number model in your list should yield worse fit for the higher-number (more constrained) model.

> On Wednesday, December 9, 2020 at 12:08:25 PM UTC-5 jana...@gmail.com wrote:
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > I am trying to understand how lavaan calculates variances of a categorical endogenous variable, when the categorical output depends on a mediator variable.
> >
> > I have this simple model for illustration:
> > dat <- data.frame(a=rnorm(1000000))
> > dat$b <- dat$a*0.80+rnorm(1000000,0,0.1)
> > dat$c <- factor(ifelse(+5-2*dat$b+rnorm(1000000,0,1)>0,1,0),ordered = TRUE)
> > sem('b~a
> >             c~b', data=dat, meanstructure=TRUE)
> >
> > which gives the following output:Regressions:
> >                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
> >   b ~
> >     a                 0.800    0.000 8027.399    0.000
> >   c ~
> >     b                -1.970    0.019 -105.891    0.000
> >
> > Intercepts:
> >                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
> >    .b                -0.000    0.000   -0.538    0.590
> >    .c                 0.000
> >
> > Thresholds:
> >                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
> >     c|t1             -4.936    0.034 -146.734    0.000
> >
> > Variances:
> >                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
> >    .b                 0.010    0.000  707.188    0.000
> >    .c                 0.961
> >
> > Scales y*:
> >                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)
> >     c                 1.000
> >
> > I am wondering how the estimate for the variance of the categorical variable is calculated (marked in yellow). If b was an exogenous variable, the variance of c would be 1.
>
> The total variance of c is 1 (see its scaling factor; this is the default: parameterization = "delta").  The residual variance of c is thus 1 minus its R-squared (variance explained by its only predictor: b).  Because b is endogenous, its total variance is not a model parameter, so the R-squared is a sum of 2 components:
> the squared direct effect of b times b's residual variance
> the squared indirect effect of a (via b) times a's variance

messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of Latent Response Fitted Means in an Ordinal CFA
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of Latent Response Fitted Means in an Ordinal CFA
messages.body_plain:
> In a model using the delta parametrization constraints, the fitted.values() command returns our model-implied matrix, the means (of the assumed latent normal variables) and the thresholds.

Regardless of parameterization, fitted() returns the model-implied polychoric correlations, standardized means, and standardized thresholds.

> how can these fitted latent means be interpreted?

Means of standardized variables are always 0.

> How can we evaluate the fit of these means

We can only fit a model to reproduce what we observed.  With categorical items, we are only reproducing the estimated polychoric correlations and standardized thresholds that we "observe", not any latent means or variances.

> is there a transformation that would make it comparable to the original ordinal scale (assuming that means of Likert items are interpretable)?

No, if you want to use treat the numerical weights of your Likert scale as meaningful, you treat the items as numeric rather than as ordinal.

The mean vector is returned only because it is possible to have both continuous and categorical indicators in the same model, in which case there could be nonzero model-implied means for continuous variables, which do factor into the least-squares fit function.

> Is the interpretation dependent on the level of constraints, in the context of a measurement invariance test?

Model parameters can imply different latent-response scales across contexts, assuming sufficient constraints on thresholds.  But regardless of the response scales implied by the model parameters, all model-implied covariance matrices are standardized for the categorical variables, as well as their thresholds, since we can only calculate the discrepancy between those and the "observed" counterparts that are also standardized.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> Can I use this residual variance of c to generate new data using the estimates (coefficients, intercepts, thresholds and variances) from sem?

Yes

> Meaning that I would generate the binary variable from an underlying normal distribution with a mean to the product of parent values and coefficients, and a variance equal to the one reported to the SEM output applying the threshold reported in the output?

You generate the latent responses for c as a sum of the b effect and the c residuals, then use the threshold to dichotomize it.  Your syntax below looks correct, except you would need to simulate a first (or use the same a used to fit your model, which would be consistent with fixed.x=TRUE).

> Based on the previous example, can we generate new c using the following formula:
> b= 0+ 0.8*a + rnorm(n,0, sqrt(0.01))
> c_normal= 0 -1.970*b +rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(0.961))
> c= c_normal>=th -4.936
>
> If not, how can I generate it?
> Is there any command that does this automatically?

No, but you can specify a population model using these parameters, and simulateData() can do the rest of the job for you.  Pretty easy to use paste() to construct the syntax automatically from your model's parTable() output.

# corrected chi-square differences test
  CorrDiff <- function(fit.baseline, fit.restricted) # basline = model with less degrees of freedom
  {
  Corrc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[6]] # corrected chi-square value
  MLc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[3]] # uncorrected chi-square value
  dfBase <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[4]] # degrees of freedom

  Corrc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[6]]
  MLc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[3]]
  dfRest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[4]]

  c0 <- MLc2Rest / Corrc2Rest
  c1 <- MLc2Base / Corrc2Base
  cd <- (dfRest*c0-dfBase*c1)/(dfRest-dfBase)
  CorrDiff <- (MLc2Rest-MLc2Base)/cd # corrected difference test statistic T_d^*
  dfDiff <- dfRest - dfBase
  pDiff <- 1-pchisq(CorrDiff, dfDiff)
  result <- list(Corr.chisq.difference = CorrDiff,

messages.subject: Re: Manova in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 14 Dec 2020 at 00:42, Michal Levinsky <michal....@mail.huji.ac.il> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the quick reply! You helped me a lot.
> 1+2. In other words, if I do the same analysis at Manova will I get similar results? By the way, the two ID variables are continuous, is that okay?
>

What are the ID variables?

> 3. That's not exactly what I want. What I need is actually more appropriate for inserting the variable G in interacting with each of the IDs (I want to test how each of the IDs affects the Ds compared to the two groups). But because I'll have more than two ID at the end, it's a little complicated. A second option is to add a group option to the analysis (in sem(fit, data=, group=)) and then I can see what happens to the two groups separately, but then I have no statistical reinforcement for the differences between the groups.
> any suggestions?
>

Yes, you can do a multiple groups analysis.

With two groups (a and b), something like:

Y1 ~ c(xy1_a, xy1_b) * X + c(zy1_a, zy1_a) * Z
Y2 ~ c(xy2_a, xy2_b) * X + c(zy2_a, zy2_b) * Z

Y1 ~ c(mean_1_a, mean_1_b) * 1
Y2 ~ c(mean_2_a, mean_2_b) * 1

If you want to see the effect of group (a and b) on Y1:
mean_1_a == mean_1_b

If you want to do a multivariate test of the effect of group:
mean_1_a == mean_1_b
mean_2_a == mean_2_b

Similarly, a  test of X on Y1 across groups:
xy1_a == xy1_b

A mulitivariate test oc X on Y1 AND y2.
xy1_a == xy1_b
xy2_a == xy2_b

Etc.
I find this much clearer than manova, as it's clearer what you are testing each time.

Also, instead of writing the whole model each time, you can build it from parts.

something liike:
base_model <- "
  Y1 ~ c(xy1_a, xy1_b) * X + c(zy1_a, zy1_a) * Z
  Y2 ~ c(xy2_a, xy2_b) * X + c(zy2_a, zy2_b) * Z
  "

test_group_model_y1 = paste0(base_model, "\nmean_1_a == mean_1_b")
test_group_model_y2 = paste0(base_model, "\nmean_2_a == mean_2_b")
test_group_model_mv = paste0(base_model, "
  mean_1_a == mean_1_b
  mean_2_a == mean_2_b
  ")
 etc.

Then you can fit this model. (You can even put them in a list and fit them all at once.)

(This is a great advantage of lavaan being embedded inside a programming language like R - you can write code to generate 1000 models, fit them and extract the info that you want. [I did this once when I wanted to run a best subsets regression in lavaan]).

Hope that helps,

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Latent Growth Curve Model
messages.body_plain:
Manuel

I think you are mixing contrainst based on identification methods. You are setting the marker variable identification , and using constraints like fixed variance.

Would make these changes, changes are highlighted

library(lavaan)

# * 2.1 Configural Invariance ---------------------------------------------

# note: to force this factor loading to be free, we pre-multiply it with NA, as a hint to lavaan that the value of this parameter is still unknown.
configural_boredom <- '
# measurement model

boredom_0 =~ bos1_0 + bos1_0 + bos2_0 + bos3_0 + bos4_0 + bos5_0 + bos6_0
boredom_1 =~ bos1_1 + bos1_1 + bos2_1 + bos3_1 + bos4_1 + bos5_1 + bos6_1
boredom_2 =~ bos1_2 + bos1_2 + bos2_2 + bos3_2 + bos4_2 + bos5_2 + bos6_2
fit_configural_boredom <- cfa(configural_boredom, data = df1, missing = "FIML", estimator = "MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv>=T)

summary(fit_configural_boredom, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

# * 2.2 Weak Invariance ---------------------------------------------------

# model specification (additional constraints on latent factors)
# same factor loadings for each item over time
weak_boredom <- '
# measurement model

boredom_0 =~ lambda0*bos1_0 + lambda1*bos1_0 + lambda2*bos2_0 + lambda3*bos3_0 + lambda4*bos4_0 + lambda5*bos5_0 + lambda6*bos6_0
boredom_1 =~ lambda0*bos1_1 + lambda1*bos1_1 + lambda2*bos2_1 + lambda3*bos3_1 + lambda4*bos4_1 + lambda5*bos5_1 + lambda6*bos6_1
boredom_2 =~ lambda0*bos1_2 + lambda1*bos1_2 + lambda2*bos2_2 + lambda3*bos3_2 + lambda4*bos4_2 + lambda5*bos5_2 + lambda6*bos6_2

boredom_0 ~~ 1* boredom_0
boredom_1 ~~ NA*boredom_1
boredom_2 ~~ NA*boredom_2
'
fit_weak_boredom <- cfa(weak_boredom, data = df1, missing = "FIML", estimator = "MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv>=T)

summary(fit_weak_boredom, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

# * 2.3 Strong Invariance -------------------------------------------------

# model specification (additional constraints on manifest intercepts)
strong_boredom <- '
# measurement model

boredom_0 =~ lambda0*bos1_0 + lambda1*bos1_0 + lambda2*bos2_0 + lambda3*bos3_0 + lambda4*bos4_0 + lambda5*bos5_0 + lambda6*bos6_0
boredom_1 =~ lambda0*bos1_1 + lambda1*bos1_1 + lambda2*bos2_1 + lambda3*bos3_1 + lambda4*bos4_1 + lambda5*bos5_1 + lambda6*bos6_1
boredom_2 =~ lambda0*bos1_2 + lambda1*bos1_2 + lambda2*bos2_2 + lambda3*bos3_2 + lambda4*bos4_2 + lambda5*bos5_2 + lambda6*bos6_2

boredom_0 ~~ 1* boredom_0
boredom_1 ~~ NA*boredom_1
boredom_2 ~~ NA*boredom_2
boredom_0 ~0*1
boredom_1 ~NA*1
boredom_2 ~NA*1
'
fit_strong_boredom <- cfa(strong_boredom, data = df1, missing = "FIML", estimator = "MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv>=T)

summary(fit_strong_boredom, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

############
Why are you building that function for the LRT between models? Becuase you are using the MLR estimator?
lavaan methods of nested model comparison do the correct adjust for MLR, MLM, DWLS, etc, estimator. WIth the lavTestLRT() for nested model comparison. If you go into details, you will some options for adjustsments based on the estimator

#########
Last, when you have a bagative LV variance, for which latent variable is it? If it for the Intecept or slope might be an indicationg that this is not a random parameter but should be treated as fix, which can be odd on the SEM, but its standard in growth curves in MLM.

> > > > > # 3. Model Comparison ----------------------------------------------------
> > > > >
> > > > > # * 3.1 Steinmetz, 2014 ---------------------------------------------------
> > > > >
> > > > > # corrected chi-square differences test
> > > > > CorrDiff <- function(fit.baseline, fit.restricted) # basline = model with less degrees of freedom
> > > > > {
> > > > >   Corrc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[6]] # corrected chi-square value
> > > > >   MLc2Base <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[3]] # uncorrected chi-square value
> > > > >   dfBase <- fitMeasures(fit.baseline)[[4]] # degrees of freedom
> > > > >
> > > > >   Corrc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[6]]
> > > > >   MLc2Rest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[3]]
> > > > >   dfRest <- fitMeasures(fit.restricted)[[4]]
> > > > >
> > > > >   c0 <- MLc2Rest / Corrc2Rest
> > > > >   c1 <- MLc2Base / Corrc2Base
> > > > >   cd <- (dfRest*c0-dfBase*c1)/(dfRest-dfBase)
> > > > >   CorrDiff <- (MLc2Rest-MLc2Base)/cd # corrected difference test statistic T_d^*
> > > > >   dfDiff <- dfRest - dfBase
> > > > >   pDiff <- 1-pchisq(CorrDiff, dfDiff)
> > > > >   result <- list(Corr.chisq.difference = CorrDiff,
> > > > >                  df.difference=dfDiff, p.value=pDiff)
> > > > >   return(result)
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > > # model comparison
> > > > > CorrDiff(fit_configural_boredom, fit_weak_boredom)
> > > > > CorrDiff(fit_weak_boredom, fit_strong_boredom)
> > > > > CorrDiff(fit_strong_boredom, fit_strict_boredom)

Am Mi., 16. Dez. 2020 um 17:09 Uhr schrieb Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com>:

> > Can I use this residual variance of c to generate new data using the estimates (coefficients, intercepts, thresholds and variances) from sem?
>
> Yes
>
> > Meaning that I would generate the binary variable from an underlying normal distribution with a mean to the product of parent values and coefficients, and a variance equal to the one reported to the SEM output applying the threshold reported in the output?
>
> You generate the latent responses for c as a sum of the b effect and the c residuals, then use the threshold to dichotomize it.  Your syntax below looks correct, except you would need to simulate a first (or use the same a used to fit your model, which would be consistent with fixed.x=TRUE).
>
> > Based on the previous example, can we generate new c using the following formula:
> > b= 0+ 0.8*a + rnorm(n,0, sqrt(0.01))
> > c_normal= 0 -1.970*b +rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(0.961))
> > c= c_normal>=th -4.936
> >
> > If not, how can I generate it?
> > Is there any command that does this automatically?
>
> No, but you can specify a population model using these parameters, and simulateData() can do the rest of the job for you.  Pretty easy to use paste() to construct the syntax automatically from your model's parTable() output.
